name: Credentials in Network Shares — Discovery & Detection
description: Credentials frequently exposed in network share scripts (.ps1, .bat, .cmd, .ini, .config) accessible to all domain users. Common in environments where admins leave credential-bearing scripts in shares open to 'Everyone' or 'Domain Users'. Detection: monitor for bulk SMB connections (one-to-many from workstation), logon events from unexpected sources.
notes:
=== ATTACK ===
# Step 1: Find non-default accessible shares across domain (PowerView)
Invoke-ShareFinder -domain <DOMAIN> -ExcludeStandard -CheckShareAccess
  → Excludes C$, IPC$ (standard shares)
  → Only returns shares the current user has read access to
  → Note: hidden shares (ending in $) not shown in Explorer but accessible by UNC path

# Step 2: Navigate to share and search for credentials
cd \\<SERVER>\<SHARE>$

# findstr /m = show only matching filenames
# findstr /s = recursive subdirectory search
# findstr /i = case-insensitive
findstr /m /s /i "pass" *.bat
findstr /m /s /i "pass" *.cmd
findstr /m /s /i "pass" *.ini
findstr /m /s /i "pass" *.config
findstr /m /s /i "pass" *.ps1

# Remove /m to see the matching line (not just filename)
findstr /s /i "pw" *.config

# Search for domain name (catches 'net use' / 'runas' credential patterns)
findstr /m /s /i "<DOMAIN_NETBIOS>" *.ps1
findstr /s /i "<DOMAIN_NETBIOS>" *.ps1
  → Finds: net use E: \\DC1\sharedScripts /user:<DOMAIN>\Administrator <password>

WARNING: findstr with these args is flagged by Windows Defender as suspicious behavior

# Automated tool alternative: SauronEye
# https://github.com/vivami/SauronEye — parses collections of files for matching words

=== DETECTION ===
One-to-many SMB connections:
  → Single workstation connecting to 100s/1000s of machines = Invoke-ShareFinder scanning
  → Alert on abnormal SMB fan-out from non-server workstations

Event 4624 (successful logon) / 4625 (failed logon):
  → Privileged account (e.g., Administrator) authenticating from workstation
  → Correlate source IP vs. PAW (Privileged Access Workstation)

Event 4768 (Kerberos TGT):
  → Admin account TGT requested from unexpected IP

Honeypot technique:
  → Create realistic-looking script with fake service account password
  → Account is still active with old password (2+ years, last-modified AFTER file mod date)
  → Any 4625/4771/4776 for this account = alert

Connect to hidden share via smbclient (from Kali)

recommended.note: Credentials also stored in AD object properties (Description, Info fields).
GPP passwords — another SYSVOL-based credential exposure path.

defense.why_it_works: Admins frequently leave credential-bearing scripts (.ps1/.bat/.cmd/.ini/.config) on network shares readable by 'Everyone' or 'Domain Users'. Any domain user can browse the shares and grep them for passwords — often for privileged accounts embedded in net-use/runas lines.
defense.prerequisites: Any valid domain user with read access to non-default shares.
defense.impact: Cleartext credentials — frequently for service or admin accounts — enabling authentication and lateral movement.
defense.detection: One-to-many SMB fan-out: a single workstation connecting to hundreds/thousands of machines indicates Invoke-ShareFinder scanning. Event 4624/4625 for a privileged account authenticating from a workstation, and 4768 (TGT) for an admin account from an unexpected IP.
defense.artifacts: Abnormal SMB fan-out from a non-server workstation; findstr /s /i recursive search execution (flagged by Windows Defender); a honeypot script with a fake service-account password firing 4625/4771/4776 on any login.
defense.prevention: Restrict share ACLs (no 'Everyone'/'Domain Users' on credential-bearing shares); never store passwords in scripts on shares; monitor for SMB fan-out and privileged logons from workstations; deploy PAWs for admin logons.
defense.misconfiguration: IT staff store scripts, configuration files, or documents containing plaintext credentials on SMB shares that are readable by all domain users (SYSVOL, NETLOGON, or file server shares with 'Everyone: Read'). These credentials — often service account passwords, API keys, or admin passwords left in batch files — are accessible to any authenticated domain user.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# SMB share readable by all domain users:
# \\fileserver\IT\scripts\deploy.bat
# Contents:
net use Z: \\server\share /user:CORP\svc_deploy P@ssw0rd123  # cleartext password

# SYSVOL scripts with embedded credentials:
# \\corp.local\SYSVOL\corp.local\scripts\logon.bat
net user administrator TempAdminPass2023! /domain  # domain admin password!

# Config files:
# \\server\configs\web.config: connectionString containing DB password
defense.secure_config:
# 1. Audit shares for credentials:
# PowerShell — search for password strings in SMB shares:
Get-ChildItem '\\corp.local\SYSVOL' -Recurse -Include '*.bat','*.ps1','*.xml','*.config' |
    Select-String -Pattern 'password|passwd|pwd|credentials|secret' |
    Select-Object Path, LineNumber, Line

# 2. Replace hardcoded credentials with proper secrets management:
# Use gMSA for service accounts (no stored password needed)
# Use Windows Credential Manager / DPAPI for interactive scripts
# Use a PAM solution (CyberArk, HashiCorp Vault) for privileged credentials

# 3. Restrict share permissions:
# Remove 'Everyone: Read' from administrative shares
# Use security groups with need-to-know membership
# Enable access-based enumeration (users only see shares they can access)

# 4. Monitor with DLP or file activity monitoring:
# Alert on access to files containing password keywords
